code-capacity.title: Calculate server capacity
code-capacity.summary: A function is a reusable piece of code that turns inputs into an output. In JavaScript, return sends the result back. We will use one to estimate how many servers a service needs.
code-capacity.example: Math.ceil(2.5) returns 3. Rounding up matters because you cannot run half a server.
code-capacity.takeaway: Divide incoming requests per second by the capacity of one server, then round up. Both inputs use the same unit.
code-capacity.instruction: Complete serversNeeded(requestsPerSecond, capacityPerServer). Return the smallest whole number of servers that can handle the traffic. Requests are non-negative and capacity is always positive.
code-capacity.hint: Use Math.ceil(requestsPerSecond / capacityPerServer). Zero traffic needs zero servers in this simplified model.

code-routing.title: Route the next request
code-routing.summary: Round-robin routing takes turns across servers. An array is an ordered list; JavaScript indexes start at 0. The remainder operator (%) wraps a request number back to the start of that list.
code-routing.example: For three servers, request indexes 0, 1, 2, 3 use server indexes 0, 1, 2, 0. For example, 3 % 3 is 0.
code-routing.takeaway: Use servers[index] to read an array item. Return null if the array is empty, because no server is available.
code-routing.instruction: Complete pickServer(servers, requestIndex). Return the server for this zero-based request index using round-robin routing, or null when servers is empty. The index is a non-negative integer.
code-routing.hint: Check servers.length first. Otherwise return servers[requestIndex % servers.length].

tests.label: First request goes to server a
Fourth request wraps around to a

code-cache.title: Read through a cache
code-cache.summary: A cache lookup checks for a saved value before doing slower work. JavaScript objects hold key-value pairs. Object.hasOwn(object, key) tells you whether a key exists, even when its value is 0 or an empty string.
code-cache.example: The cached value 0 is still a hit. Testing if (cache[key]) would incorrectly treat it as missing.
code-cache.takeaway: Check whether a key exists, not whether its value is truthy. Use the database as the fallback on a miss.
code-cache.instruction: Complete readValue(cache, database, key). Return the cached value if the cache owns the key. Otherwise return the database value, or null if neither object owns it. Values are strings or numbers.
code-cache.hint: Check Object.hasOwn(cache, key), then Object.hasOwn(database, key), then return null.

tests.label: Cache hit wins over the database copy
Zero is a valid cached value
Empty string is a valid cached value

code-healthy-router.title: Build a health-aware router
code-healthy-router.summary: A router sends work to a server that can handle it. A health check lets it skip unavailable servers instead of repeatedly sending requests to them.
code-healthy-router.example: With servers A (down), B (healthy), and C (healthy), request indexes 0, 1, 2 go to B, C, B.
code-healthy-router.takeaway: Filter healthy servers first; apply round-robin to that filtered list.
code-healthy-router.instruction: Return the id of a healthy server using requestIndex modulo the number of healthy servers. Preserve input order. Return null if none are healthy. Inputs use a nonnegative integer index.
code-healthy-router.hint: Filter healthy servers first; apply round-robin to that filtered list.

code-unique-ids.title: Remove duplicate IDs
code-unique-ids.summary: Deduplication keeps one copy of each identity when the same item appears multiple times. Identity, rather than arrival count, determines whether work is new.
code-unique-ids.takeaway: A Set remembers whether a value has appeared.
code-unique-ids.instruction: Return unique string IDs in first-seen order. Do not change the input array.
code-unique-ids.hint: A Set remembers whether a value has appeared.

code-count-events.title: Count event types
code-count-events.summary: A frequency table maps each distinct value to the number of times it occurs. It is useful for counting requests, errors, or event categories.
code-count-events.takeaway: Use a Map while counting, then convert it to an object.
code-count-events.instruction: Return an object mapping each string event type to its count. Treat every string as a valid key, including reserved object names.
code-count-events.hint: Use a Map while counting, then convert it to an object.

code-group-jobs.title: Group work by tenant
code-group-jobs.summary: A tenant is one customer or organization sharing a service. Grouping work by tenant helps schedule, count, and isolate each customer’s workload.
code-group-jobs.example: Jobs a(t1), b(t2), c(t1) become t1: [a, c], t2: [b].
code-group-jobs.takeaway: Each tenant needs its own array; a Map avoids special object-key behavior.
code-group-jobs.instruction: Return an object mapping tenant strings to arrays of job IDs in arrival order. Do not mutate jobs.
code-group-jobs.hint: Each tenant needs its own array; a Map avoids special object-key behavior.

code-batch-dedup.title: Build a deduplicating batcher
code-batch-dedup.summary: A batch groups several items into one unit of work. Deduplicating before batching avoids performing the same logical job twice in one submission.
code-batch-dedup.example: IDs [a, b, a, c] with a batch size of 2 become [[a, b], [c]].
code-batch-dedup.takeaway: Deduplicate first, then take slices without changing the input.
code-batch-dedup.instruction: Return batches of unique string IDs, preserving first-seen order. Each batch has at most size items. Return [] if size is not a positive integer.
code-batch-dedup.hint: Deduplicate first, then take slices without changing the input.

code-link-service.title: Build a tiny link service
code-link-service.summary: A request handler turns an incoming action into a response. In this model, GET reads a saved destination and PUT changes it. A cache speeds up repeated reads, while the records object is the source of truth.
code-link-service.example: GET go → /old. PUT go /new → saved. GET go must now return /new, even if /old was cached.
code-link-service.takeaway: A fast read path is useful only when updates preserve correctness. Keep the source of truth and invalidate stale copies.
code-link-service.instruction: Process requests in order. GET: check the cache first; on a miss count one database read, return {status:302, location:value} for a stored key and cache it, or {status:404} without caching a miss. PUT: store value, invalidate that key in the cache, and return {status:204}. Other methods return {status:405} without reading or changing records. Start with an empty cache. Return {records, responses, databaseReads}. Keys and values are strings, including keys that match JavaScript object names. This is an in-memory simulation, not a network server. Preserve both inputs.
code-link-service.hint: Try new Map(Object.entries(initial)) for records and a separate Map for the cache. A Map stores keys without inherited object properties. Use has/get/set/delete inside a for...of loop; return Object.fromEntries(records). Count only GET cache misses.

tests.label: First read fills cache; second read is a cache hit
Missing keys return 404 and are not cached
Write, read, update, then read the fresh destination
An update invalidates only its own key
Unsupported methods do not read or change records
Inherited object names are not stored links
Object-name keys and empty destinations remain valid data

code-validate-limit.title: Validate a request limit
code-validate-limit.summary: Input validation checks whether a request value has the shape and range an API accepts. It stops ambiguous or invalid inputs before they reach the main operation.
code-validate-limit.example: A limit of 25 is accepted; 0, "25", and 2.5 are rejected.
code-validate-limit.takeaway: Use Number.isInteger, then check both bounds.
code-validate-limit.instruction: Return the numeric limit only if it is an integer between 1 and 100 inclusive. Return null otherwise. Do not coerce strings.
code-validate-limit.hint: Use Number.isInteger, then check both bounds.

code-normalize-event.title: Normalize an incoming event
code-normalize-event.summary: Normalization converts accepted input into one predictable representation. Validation must still reject values that cannot be interpreted safely.
code-normalize-event.takeaway: Check types before calling string methods. Keep identifiers case-sensitive.
code-normalize-event.instruction: Return only {id, type}, trimming both string fields and lowercasing type. Return null for non-object input, missing/non-string fields, or fields that become empty.
code-normalize-event.hint: Check types before calling string methods. Keep identifiers case-sensitive.

code-page-results.title: Return a bounded page
code-page-results.summary: Pagination splits a result set into bounded responses. A predictable offset and limit keep one request from returning an unbounded amount of data.
code-page-results.example: An offset of 2 and limit of 2 returns the third and fourth items.
code-page-results.takeaway: Validate the bounds before using slice.
code-page-results.instruction: Return items.slice(offset, offset + limit) for nonnegative integer offset and positive integer limit. Return [] for invalid bounds. Do not mutate items.
code-page-results.hint: Validate the bounds before using slice.

code-cache-ttl.title: Read a cache with expiry
code-cache-ttl.concept: What is a time to live?
code-cache-ttl.summary: A time to live limits how long a cached value remains usable. Expiration is a boundary decision: a record whose expiry equals the current time is already expired.
code-cache-ttl.example: At now=100, an entry expiring at 101 is usable; one expiring at 100 is not.
code-cache-ttl.takeaway: Check key existence and expiration separately from the cached value.
code-cache-ttl.instruction: Return {hit: true, value} when cache has its own key and expiresAt > now. Otherwise return {hit: false, value: null}. Cached false, 0, and null are valid hits.
code-cache-ttl.hint: Check key existence and expiration separately from the cached value.

code-fixed-window.title: Apply a fixed-window limit
code-fixed-window.concept: What is a fixed-window rate limit?
code-fixed-window.summary: A fixed-window limiter counts requests in a time bucket. Requests in a new bucket start with a fresh count; rejected requests do not consume another slot.
code-fixed-window.example: A count of 2 with a limit of 3 accepts one request and returns a count of 3.
code-fixed-window.takeaway: Decide the effective count first, then increment only when accepting.
code-fixed-window.instruction: Given {window, count}, the current integer window, and a positive integer limit, return {allowed, state}. Reset count when the window changes. Never mutate the input state.
code-fixed-window.hint: Decide the effective count first, then increment only when accepting.

code-token-bucket.title: Refill a token bucket
code-token-bucket.summary: A token bucket accumulates permission to perform work at a fixed rate, up to a capacity. A request consumes tokens only when enough are available.
code-token-bucket.example: Two tokens plus three seconds at two tokens per second refill to eight, before applying a capacity cap.
code-token-bucket.takeaway: Cap after refilling. A rejected request keeps the refilled balance.
code-token-bucket.instruction: For nonnegative numeric inputs and positive capacity, refill tokens by elapsedSeconds * refillPerSecond, cap at capacity, then spend cost if affordable. Return {allowed, tokens}.
code-token-bucket.hint: Cap after refilling. A rejected request keeps the refilled balance.

code-sliding-window.title: Count a sliding window
code-sliding-window.concept: What is a sliding time window?
code-sliding-window.summary: A sliding window follows the current time instead of resetting at fixed boundaries. Defining its endpoints prevents off-by-one errors at expiration.
code-sliding-window.example: For now=100 and width=10, timestamps greater than 90 and at most 100 count.
code-sliding-window.takeaway: Use a strict lower bound and an inclusive upper bound.
code-sliding-window.instruction: Count timestamps in the interval (now - width, now]. Inputs use a positive numeric width. Ignore future timestamps.
code-sliding-window.hint: Use a strict lower bound and an inclusive upper bound.

code-admit-batch.title: Enforce a per-tenant budget
code-admit-batch.summary: Admission control decides which work can enter a system. Separate tenant budgets keep one customer’s burst from consuming another customer’s allowance.
code-admit-batch.example: With a limit of 2, the third request from tenant A is rejected even if tenant B has used none.
code-admit-batch.takeaway: Copy counts into a Map and update only accepted requests.
code-admit-batch.instruction: Process requests [{id, tenant}] in order, starting from counts. Return {accepted, rejected, counts} using request IDs and a positive integer per-tenant limit. Preserve inputs and safely handle any tenant name.
code-admit-batch.hint: Copy counts into a Map and update only accepted requests.

code-idempotency.title: Recognize a retried operation
code-idempotency.summary: An idempotent operation has the same effect when repeated. An idempotency key identifies retries of one logical request so the stored result can be reused.
code-idempotency.example: A payment retry with an existing key should return the saved result without charging again.
code-idempotency.takeaway: Existence matters even when the stored result is null or false.
code-idempotency.instruction: If records has its own key, return {execute: false, result: records[key]}. Otherwise return {execute: true, result: null}. Do not modify records.
code-idempotency.hint: Existence matters even when the stored result is null or false.

code-version-write.title: Reject a stale write
code-version-write.summary: Optimistic concurrency checks that a record has not changed since it was read. A version mismatch rejects a stale update instead of silently replacing newer work.
code-version-write.example: A client expecting version 3 cannot update a record that has already reached version 4.
code-version-write.takeaway: Compare the version before constructing the updated record.
code-version-write.instruction: Given {version, value}, expectedVersion, and a new value, return {updated, record}. Increment version on a match. Otherwise return the unchanged record. Do not mutate input.
code-version-write.hint: Compare the version before constructing the updated record.

code-reconcile-records.title: Reconcile versioned records
code-reconcile-records.summary: Reconciliation combines copies of data using an explicit conflict rule. Versions can identify newer records, but equal versions still need a defined policy.
code-reconcile-records.example: For the same ID, version 5 replaces version 4. This exercise keeps the local copy when versions are equal.
code-reconcile-records.takeaway: Track the winning record in a Map, then sort a new array.
code-reconcile-records.instruction: Merge local and remote arrays of {id, version, value}. Keep the highest version per ID; keep the first encountered record on ties. Process local first. Return records sorted by id. Do not mutate inputs.
code-reconcile-records.hint: Track the winning record in a Map, then sort a new array.

code-apply-events.title: Apply events exactly once locally
code-apply-events.summary: A projection derives current state from a sequence of events. Remembering applied event IDs prevents a retry from affecting the projection twice within this state store.
code-apply-events.example: Starting at 10, event a(+3), a(+3), b(-2) produces 11 when a is counted once.
code-apply-events.takeaway: Initialize a Set from seen and add each new ID before applying its delta.
code-apply-events.instruction: Given {total, seen}, apply events [{id, delta}] once per unseen ID. Return a new {total, seen}, preserving first-seen order. Inputs contain numeric deltas and string IDs. This is local deduplication, not a distributed exactly-once guarantee.
code-apply-events.hint: Initialize a Set from seen and add each new ID before applying its delta.

code-backoff.title: Calculate bounded retry delays
code-backoff.summary: Exponential backoff increases the wait between failed attempts. A cap prevents the delay from growing without bound. Production systems often add jitter so clients do not retry together.
code-backoff.example: With a 100 ms base, attempts 0, 1, and 2 wait 100, 200, and 400 ms.
code-backoff.takeaway: The first retry uses attempt 0, so its delay equals the base.
code-backoff.instruction: Return min(capMs, baseMs * 2 ** attempt) for a nonnegative integer attempt and positive numeric base/cap. Jitter is deliberately excluded from this deterministic exercise.
code-backoff.hint: The first retry uses attempt 0, so its delay equals the base.

code-ready-jobs.title: Schedule only ready jobs
code-ready-jobs.summary: A delayed job has an earliest execution time. A scheduler should run only due work, using a deterministic order when multiple jobs become ready together.
code-ready-jobs.example: At now=50, jobs scheduled at 40 and 50 are ready; a job scheduled at 51 must wait.
code-ready-jobs.takeaway: Filter before sorting, then take a bounded slice.
code-ready-jobs.instruction: Return up to limit ready job IDs, sorted by readyAt and then id. Include readyAt === now. limit is a nonnegative integer. Do not change jobs.
code-ready-jobs.hint: Filter before sorting, then take a bounded slice.

code-dead-letter.title: Separate retries from dead letters
code-dead-letter.summary: A dead-letter queue holds work that cannot be processed after its retry budget. It preserves failed jobs for inspection instead of retrying forever or silently discarding them.
code-dead-letter.example: With a maximum of 3 attempts, a job at attempt 2 can retry; a job at attempt 3 is dead-lettered.
code-dead-letter.instruction: Partition failed jobs [{id, attempts}] into {retry, deadLetter} ID arrays. attempts counts attempts already made. Jobs with attempts >= maxAttempts go to deadLetter. Preserve input order.

code-worker-plan.title: Build a bounded worker plan
code-worker-plan.concept: What is a worker scheduling plan?
code-worker-plan.summary: A worker plan decides which queued jobs may execute now, which must wait, and which have exhausted their retry budget. Capacity and retry limits apply before work starts.
code-worker-plan.example: A due job with retries left may run; a future job waits; a job at its retry limit goes to dead letters.
code-worker-plan.takeaway: Separate exhausted jobs, select eligible work with a stable sort, then classify the remaining IDs.
code-worker-plan.instruction: Given jobs [{id, readyAt, attempts}], now, nonnegative integer capacity, and positive maxAttempts, return {run, waiting, deadLetter} IDs. Classify exhausted jobs first. Select due jobs by readyAt then id, up to capacity. Preserve original order in waiting and deadLetter. Do not mutate input.
code-worker-plan.hint: Separate exhausted jobs, select eligible work with a stable sort, then classify the remaining IDs.

lesson-llm-intro.title: Introduction to LLMs
lesson-llm-intro.concept: What is a large language model?
lesson-llm-intro.summary: A large language model (LLM) is a neural network trained to predict tokens in language. By repeating that prediction one token at a time, it can draft text, summarize documents, answer questions, transform structured data, and help call software tools.
lesson-llm-intro.example: In plain language, an LLM is a powerful pattern generator. It can produce a fluent answer without possessing an independent source of truth, so useful systems surround it with context, evidence, validation, and clear authority boundaries.
lesson-llm-intro.takeaway: An LLM generates a likely continuation from its model weights and retained context. A likely continuation is not automatically a true claim or an authorized action.

models.title: Trace a next-token decision
Decide whether an answer may leave the system

lesson-transformers.title: Transformer Architecture
lesson-transformers.summary: A Transformer is a neural-network architecture that moves information between sequence positions with attention. Each position creates a query, compares it with keys from positions it is allowed to read, and blends their values into a new contextual representation.
lesson-transformers.example: In plain language: every token asks, "Which other tokens matter to what I mean right now?" The answer changes at every layer and attention head.
lesson-transformers.takeaway: The core invariant is attention may combine only information allowed by the model's task contract. An encoder may read both directions; an autoregressive decoder must hide future tokens; an encoder-decoder model adds cross-attention from generated tokens to encoded input.

models.title: Trace what one attention head can read
Budget decoder KV cache before admitting traffic

lesson-llms.title: LLM Models & Families
lesson-llms.concept: What is a large language model?
lesson-llms.summary: A large language model (LLM) is a neural network trained to predict tokens in sequences. A token may be a word, part of a word, punctuation, or another encoded unit. During generation, the model repeatedly estimates what token should come next, samples or selects one, appends it to the context, and continues.
lesson-llms.example: In plain language: an LLM is a powerful pattern model for language and other tokenized data. It can draft, transform, classify, summarize, reason over supplied context, and call tools, but its next-token objective does not guarantee truth, policy compliance, or successful task completion.
lesson-llms.takeaway: Product behavior comes from the complete model bundle and request path, not from a model name alone. The base weights, adaptation, prompt, retrieved evidence, tools, decoding settings, safety controls, runtime, and release policy all affect the result.

models.title: Put each change in the least persistent layer
Fit an inference path to a real request envelope

lesson-tokenization-fundamentals.title: Tokenization Fundamentals
lesson-tokenization-fundamentals.summary: Tokenization is the versioned process that turns text into a sequence of integer token IDs. A token can represent a word, part of a word, punctuation, whitespace, a byte sequence, or a control marker.
lesson-tokenization-fundamentals.example: In plain language, a model cannot read a string directly. Its tokenizer converts the string into IDs, and each ID selects one learned vector from the model's embedding table. The order of those vectors becomes the model's input sequence.
lesson-tokenization-fundamentals.takeaway: A tokenizer and a model checkpoint form one contract. Normalization rules, vocabulary entries, token IDs, special tokens, and templates must match what the model saw during training. A valid ID from a different vocabulary can select the wrong embedding without producing an obvious error.

models.title: Trace a teaching tokenizer contract
Fit content without hiding information loss

lesson-bpe-algorithm.title: BPE Algorithm Deep Dive
lesson-bpe-algorithm.summary: Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) is a vocabulary-learning algorithm that repeatedly replaces the most frequent adjacent symbol pair with one new symbol. In tokenization, those learned symbols become reusable subword pieces such as low, ing, or _user.
lesson-bpe-algorithm.example: BPE sits between character and word tokenization. It can represent unseen words from smaller pieces while giving frequent patterns shorter sequences. That balance matters because every token consumes model context and inference work, but every vocabulary entry also consumes an embedding row and must be learned from data.
lesson-bpe-algorithm.takeaway: The normalizer, boundary rules, ordered merge table, token-to-ID map, special tokens, and model checkpoint form one contract. Applying the same merges in a different order, or assigning a familiar piece a different ID, changes what the model receives.

models.title: Train a merge vocabulary from corpus evidence
Trace encoding and protect the token-ID contract

lesson-production-tokenization.title: Production Tokenization Systems
lesson-production-tokenization.concept: What is a production tokenization system?
lesson-production-tokenization.summary: A production tokenization system is the bounded, observable path that turns application text into the exact token IDs, masks, offsets, and control markers expected by a deployed model. It may run inside each model worker or behind a dedicated service, but it always sits on the model's correctness boundary.
lesson-production-tokenization.example: In a notebook, correct output for one string may be enough. In production, the same tokenizer must handle concurrent traffic, hostile or malformed input, multiple languages, cache isolation, versioned artifacts, and rollbacks without silently changing what the model receives.
lesson-production-tokenization.takeaway: Release the tokenizer, model checkpoint, prompt template, normalization rules, and special-token IDs as one immutable contract. A faster tokenizer that maps text to different IDs is not an optimization; it is a different model interface.

models.title: Size a bounded tokenization hot path
Gate a tokenizer and model release

lesson-prompt-engineering.title: Prompt Engineering
lesson-prompt-engineering.summary: Prompt engineering is the practice of turning a product task into a clear, bounded input contract for a language model. That contract tells the model what job to perform, which evidence it may use, which rules it must follow, and what output a caller can validate.
lesson-prompt-engineering.example: In plain language, a model cannot reliably recover requirements that the application never supplied. Prompt engineering makes those requirements visible and testable instead of relying on clever wording or luck.
lesson-prompt-engineering.takeaway: A prompt version is production-ready only when its behavior is measured on representative inputs and every required safety, correctness, and format gate passes. A fluent example or a higher average score cannot replace that evidence.

models.title: Assemble a prompt contract
Decide whether a prompt version can ship

lesson-conversational-ai.title: Conversational AI
lesson-conversational-ai.summary: Conversational AI is a system that accepts natural-language turns, assembles bounded context, generates or executes an answer, and preserves only the state needed for useful continuity. The product is not just a chat box around a model. It is a stateful request protocol with identity, memory, retrieval, tools, streaming, safety, and terminal outcomes.
lesson-conversational-ai.example: In plain language, the assistant should understand a follow-up without pretending it remembers information that was never stored, has expired, belongs to another user, or no longer fits in the context window.
lesson-conversational-ai.takeaway: The core invariant is every turn must be attributable to one authorized session, and every response or side effect must reflect the context and outcome that actually occurred. A missing memory, failed tool, cancelled stream, or blocked answer cannot be rewritten as success.

models.title: Follow one conversational turn
Build a conversational turn that fits

lesson-function-calling.title: Function Calling
lesson-function-calling.summary: Function calling is a pattern in which a language model proposes a named tool and structured arguments, then application code decides whether and how to execute that proposal. The tool might read an order, calculate a price, reserve inventory, or send a message.
lesson-function-calling.example: The model does not call your database or API by itself. It produces data shaped like {"name":"lookup_order","arguments":{"orderId":"ord_1842"}}. Your application validates that data, checks the caller's authority, executes trusted code, and returns a structured result for the model to explain.
lesson-function-calling.takeaway: Function calling matters because generated text can now influence real systems. A fluent answer can be merely wrong; a poorly controlled tool call can expose another tenant's data, repeat a charge, or delete a record.

models.title: Trace a proposal through schema and policy
Recover a timeout without repeating the user's intent

lesson-smart-text-completion.title: Smart Text Completion
lesson-smart-text-completion.summary: Smart text completion proposes a short continuation while a person is actively writing. It is a selective prediction product: the system may generate several candidates, but it shows text only when one candidate is useful, timely, current, and allowed by policy.
lesson-smart-text-completion.example: This is different from a chatbot response. The writer already owns the document and can keep typing at any moment. A completion is a temporary proposal attached to one exact cursor state, not an instruction to replace user text.
lesson-smart-text-completion.takeaway: The feature matters because a weak suggestion consumes attention even when it is ignored.

models.title: Trade context and model depth against a visible suggestion
Decide whether a completion bundle should expand

lesson-translation-systems.title: Translation Systems
lesson-translation-systems.concept: What is a machine translation system?
lesson-translation-systems.summary: A machine translation system turns a message in a source language into a target-language message that preserves the intended meaning. The model generates the words, but the production system also detects language, protects names and placeholders, applies approved terminology, estimates quality, and decides whether the result is safe to release.
lesson-translation-systems.example: Translation is not word substitution. Word order, grammatical features, idioms, context, and writing direction can all change between languages. A fluent sentence can still be wrong if it drops a negation, changes a number, invents a fact, or mistranslates a required product term.
lesson-translation-systems.takeaway: Core invariant: release the target text only when its meaning and protected facts remain attributable to the source. A high model score never overrides a missing number, broken placeholder, unsafe addition, or unsupported language pair.

models.title: Trace a candidate through decoding and constraints
Decide whether a translation bundle can ship

lesson-rag-systems.title: Building RAG Systems
lesson-rag-systems.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) combines information retrieval with language generation. Before an LLM answers, the application retrieves relevant documents and places them in the model's context so the answer can use current, private, or domain-specific evidence.
lesson-rag-systems.example: In plain language: RAG gives an LLM an open-book reference for each question. It improves grounding without retraining the model and can attach sources to claims.
lesson-rag-systems.takeaway: Use the full lesson’s worked examples and interactive labs to explore the trade-offs behind these questions.

lesson-rag.title: RAG Implementation
lesson-rag.summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is a system pattern that finds external evidence at request time and gives that evidence to a language model before it writes an answer. The model supplies language and reasoning; the retrieval system supplies current, private, or domain-specific facts.
lesson-rag.example: In plain language: RAG is an open-book workflow. It searches first, reads a small set of relevant passages, and answers from those passages. This can make knowledge easier to update and answers easier to inspect without retraining the model.
lesson-rag.takeaway: The core invariant is an answer is only as trustworthy as its authorized evidence. A fluent response is not grounded when the system retrieved the wrong document, crossed an access boundary, omitted a necessary fact, or cited text that does not support the claim.

lesson-advanced-rag.title: Advanced RAG Patterns
lesson-advanced-rag.summary: Advanced retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) patterns add a deliberate planning, representation, fusion, hierarchy, or evidence-checking stage when one bounded retrieval pass repeatedly misses the evidence a question needs.
lesson-advanced-rag.example: In plain language: basic RAG searches once. An advanced pipeline may rewrite a difficult question, search several ranked views, traverse a document hierarchy, or choose a retrieval branch per request. These stages do not make an answer trustworthy by themselves. They only change how candidate evidence is found and selected.
lesson-advanced-rag.takeaway: The core invariant is complexity must answer a measured retrieval failure. A fluent model, a larger context window, or more search calls cannot replace authorized, current, answer-bearing evidence.

lesson-knowledge-graphs.title: Knowledge Graphs
lesson-knowledge-graphs.summary: A knowledge graph represents facts as entities and named relationships. Instead of storing only a paragraph that says "Atlas depends on Token Service," the graph stores Atlas, Token Service, and a directed DEPENDS_ON edge between them.
lesson-knowledge-graphs.example: That structure matters when an application must answer more than a keyword question. It can follow paths, enforce types, preserve where each fact came from, and explain why two entities are connected. A graph does not make extracted text true by itself: identity resolution, relation validation, provenance, and access control determine whether its answers deserve trust.
lesson-knowledge-graphs.takeaway: The core invariant is that every accepted node and edge remains traceable to evidence, policy, and time. The language model may propose or explain facts; it must not silently promote an unsupported claim into graph truth.

models.title: Build the graph without collapsing the wrong identities

lesson-rag-systems-foundation.title: RAG Systems Foundation
lesson-rag-systems-foundation.summary: A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system is an application pipeline that finds external evidence for a question, places selected evidence in a language model's context, and asks the model to answer from that evidence.
lesson-rag-systems-foundation.example: In plain language, RAG gives the model a small, authorized, open-book packet for each request. The model still generates the answer, but the facts should come from identifiable sources that can be updated without retraining the model.
lesson-rag-systems-foundation.takeaway: RAG matters when an application needs private, domain-specific, or changing knowledge. It does not make a model truthful by itself. Core invariant: every factual claim must be traceable to authorized, versioned evidence that was valid for that request, or the system must abstain or contain the failure.

lesson-rag-architecture-deep-dive.title: RAG Architecture Deep Dive
lesson-rag-architecture-deep-dive.summary: A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) architecture is the complete system that finds evidence for a question, places a bounded set of that evidence in a model prompt, and decides whether the resulting answer is safe to release.
lesson-rag-architecture-deep-dive.example: In plain language: the model does not search the whole knowledge base itself. A retrieval system selects a small, authorized evidence packet first. The model must answer from that packet or admit that the evidence is insufficient.
lesson-rag-architecture-deep-dive.takeaway: The core invariant is no evidence, no grounded claim. A fluent answer is not proof that retrieval found the right source, that the user may see it, or that the source is current.

lesson-vector-database-implementation.title: Vector Database Implementation
lesson-vector-database-implementation.summary: A vector database stores records alongside numeric embeddings and retrieves records whose vectors are near a query vector. The embedding represents learned features; the database owns identity, metadata, indexing, filtering, updates, replication, and the query contract around those numbers.
lesson-vector-database-implementation.example: In plain language: an embedding model decides how items are represented, while the vector database decides how those representations become searchable production state.
lesson-vector-database-implementation.takeaway: The core invariant is return authorized, version-compatible evidence within a measured recall, freshness, and latency contract. A fast nearest-neighbor response is wrong if it searches a mixed embedding space, drops relevant items, exposes another tenant's record, or serves a deleted chunk.

lesson-langchain-production.title: LangChain Production
lesson-langchain-production.summary: Production LangChain is the practice of operating a LangChain application as a reliable software system, not merely getting a model call to work. LangChain supplies model, tool, agent, and middleware abstractions; LangGraph supplies lower-level stateful orchestration; LangSmith can supply tracing, evaluation, and deployment services.
lesson-langchain-production.example: In plain language: the framework helps connect the steps, but your application still owns the contract. It must bound what a run may do, identify its state, survive dependency and worker failures, expose evidence, and reach a user-visible terminal outcome.
lesson-langchain-production.takeaway: The core invariant is every accepted run needs a bounded authority, deadline, durable identity, and observable outcome. A retry, deployment restart, or resumed thread must not silently become a second business operation.

models.title: Commit to an orchestration boundary
Recover the run, not just the process

lesson-ai-agents.title: AI Agent Architectures
lesson-ai-agents.summary: An AI agent is a software system that uses a model to decide what to do next, calls bounded tools to affect or inspect an environment, observes the result, and continues until it reaches a stopping condition.
lesson-ai-agents.example: A chatbot normally turns one request into one response. An agent adds an execution loop: it can gather evidence, choose a tool, update working state, retry a safe operation, ask for approval, or stop when the next action would exceed its authority.
lesson-ai-agents.takeaway: Agents matter when a task cannot be completed by one model response. They also create a new systems problem because generated text now influences real APIs, records, messages, and money.

lesson-model-context-protocol.title: Model Context Protocol Architecture
lesson-model-context-protocol.summary: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open protocol for connecting AI applications to external context and capabilities. It standardizes how an application discovers and uses server-provided resources, prompts, and tools over JSON-RPC instead of building a different connector contract for every integration.
lesson-model-context-protocol.example: In plain language: MCP is a shared language between an AI application and the programs that provide useful data or actions. The application remains responsible for deciding which servers to trust, which capabilities to expose, what the user approves, and how results are handled.
lesson-model-context-protocol.takeaway: The core invariant is capability is not authority. A successful handshake proves that both sides understand a protocol feature. It does not prove that the server is trustworthy, that a token has the right audience, or that a tool call is approved.

models.title: Build a usable session without confusing support for permission

lesson-agentic-ai-systems.title: Agentic AI Systems Design
lesson-agentic-ai-systems.concept: What is an agentic AI system?
lesson-agentic-ai-systems.summary: An agentic AI system is software in which a model can choose the next step in a multi-step task, use tools, inspect results, and continue until a runtime stop condition is reached. The model may help decompose a goal and propose actions, but ordinary software still owns credentials, authorization, durable state, budgets, and execution.
lesson-agentic-ai-systems.example: In plain language: a chatbot mainly produces a response. An agentic system can also choose and invoke bounded operations such as reading a case, running a test, or proposing a refund. That extra action surface can be useful, but it also lets one bad observation affect later decisions.
lesson-agentic-ai-systems.takeaway: Core invariantThe model may propose what to do next, but a deterministic runtime decides what is allowed to execute, what state becomes durable, what may be retried, and when the run must stop.

lesson-computer-use-agents.title: Computer-Use and Browser Agent Systems
lesson-computer-use-agents.summary: A computer-use agent is an AI system that observes a graphical interface, proposes mouse or keyboard actions, and uses the resulting interface state to continue a task. It can work in a browser, a desktop application, or a virtual machine even when the software has no purpose-built API.
lesson-computer-use-agents.example: In plain language: the model suggests how to use the screen, while your application captures observations, decides what is allowed, performs each action, and checks what actually happened.
lesson-computer-use-agents.takeaway: Computer use matters because graphical interfaces are stateful and only partly observable. A button can move, a modal can cover a target, a session can expire, or an apparently successful click can create an external side effect before the response is lost.

Resolve the failed boundary

lesson-personalized-genai.title: Personalized GenAI
lesson-personalized-genai.summary: Personalized generative AI adapts a response to a person's declared preferences, current task, authorized knowledge, or carefully inferred needs. The adaptation may change the answer's depth, format, examples, retrieved evidence, or specialized behavior while preserving the same product and safety rules.
lesson-personalized-genai.example: In plain language: a useful system remembers that one learner prefers worked examples, but it does not silently turn every click, private document, or old conversation into a permanent fact about that learner.
lesson-personalized-genai.takeaway: The core invariant is bounded, user-correctable adaptation: every personalized effect should come from an authorized signal, serve a declared purpose, remain inspectable, and have a working update and deletion path.

lesson-llm-serving.title: LLM Serving & APIs
lesson-llm-serving.summary: LLM serving is the production system that accepts a model request, decides whether and where to run it, generates tokens, and delivers a bounded response. It turns a trained or hosted model into a dependable product capability.
lesson-llm-serving.example: This matters because a useful answer is more than a model call. A long prompt can exhaust memory before generation begins, a slow stream can hold capacity after the user leaves, and a fallback can change what the answer is allowed to claim.
lesson-llm-serving.takeaway: The core invariant is: admission, scheduling, model execution, safety checks, and streaming must share one request identity and one deadline. Every retry, token, cache entry, fallback, and cancellation should be attributable to that same request contract.

models.title: Batching and KV-cache capacity lab
Overload and failure routing lab

lesson-token-management.title: Token Management
lesson-token-management.summary: Token management is the control system that decides how a finite model context is allocated, how much output may be generated, and how token demand is admitted, measured, and stopped in production.
lesson-token-management.example: Tokens are model-specific units, not fixed words. A request may spend them on instructions, tool definitions, conversation history, retrieved evidence, the current user input, hidden or visible reasoning, and the response. The core invariant is simple: every token must fit inside an explicit request envelope and remain attributable to a useful outcome.
lesson-token-management.takeaway: This matters for more than cost. A poor token policy can remove the evidence needed for a correct answer, leave too little room for the output, overflow a context window, exhaust token-per-minute capacity, increase queue latency, or amplify an outage through retries.

models.title: Build a context that preserves the decision

lesson-llm-inference-optimization.title: LLM Inference Optimization
lesson-llm-inference-optimization.summary: LLM inference optimization is the engineering work that makes an already-trained language model respond within a product's latency, capacity, cost, and quality limits. It changes how requests are admitted, batched, cached, scheduled, represented in memory, and decoded; it does not retrain the model's core knowledge.
lesson-llm-inference-optimization.example: In plain language: training creates the model, while inference optimization makes each request practical to serve.
lesson-llm-inference-optimization.takeaway: The core invariant is optimize the measured request path without silently breaking the answer contract. A faster kernel is not a production win if queueing gets worse, a quantized checkpoint fails the important task slice, or a cache crosses tenant boundaries.

models.title: Balance the first token against shared capacity
Pack the pool without breaking the answer contract

lesson-ai-gateway-patterns.title: AI Gateway Patterns
lesson-ai-gateway-patterns.summary: An AI gateway is a trusted service boundary between an application and one or more model-serving APIs. It authenticates the caller, binds the request to a tenant, applies policy and budget controls, chooses an eligible route, invokes a provider-specific adapter, and records what happened.
lesson-ai-gateway-patterns.example: In plain language: the application sends one product-level request, but the gateway decides whether that request may run and which tested model route can satisfy it. The gateway is not the model, and it is not just a renamed provider SDK.
lesson-ai-gateway-patterns.takeaway: This boundary matters because model calls carry more than text. They carry identity, sensitive data, token and cost exposure, deadlines, streaming connections, safety requirements, and fallback risk.

models.title: Filter routes before you optimize them
Contain a bad route before it becomes a global incident

lesson-model-serving-patterns.title: Model Serving Patterns
lesson-model-serving-patterns.summary: Model serving patterns are reusable ways to turn trained model artifacts into dependable prediction services. They define how a request is admitted, queued, batched, routed to a compatible model replica, executed, observed, and either completed or rejected.
lesson-model-serving-patterns.example: In plain language: a model server does more than call predict. It protects scarce compute while keeping the product's latency, quality, isolation, and availability promises.
lesson-model-serving-patterns.takeaway: The core invariant is admit only work the fleet can finish inside an explicit contract. Unbounded queues, blind retries, and cold replicas do not create capacity; they move failure later in the request path.

lesson-inference-time-scaling.title: Inference-Time Scaling and Reasoning Budgets
lesson-inference-time-scaling.summary: Inference-time scaling means spending additional computation while a model is answering a particular request. Instead of always making one model call, the system can let the model reason longer, generate several candidates, retrieve evidence, execute a test, ask a verifier, or escalate to a stronger model or a person.
lesson-inference-time-scaling.example: In plain language: training determines what a model can generally do; inference-time scaling decides how much effort this request deserves right now.
lesson-inference-time-scaling.takeaway: The core invariant is a bounded request budget. Every candidate, tool call, verification pass, and escalation consumes from one deadline and cost envelope. More compute is useful only when it produces evidence that improves the final decision.

models.title: Pack a bounded reasoning policy
Decide when the reasoning loop may stop

lesson-production-transformer-architectu.title: Production Transformer Architecture
lesson-production-transformer-architectu.concept: What is a production Transformer architecture?
lesson-production-transformer-architectu.summary: A production Transformer architecture is the complete execution system that turns a trained Transformer checkpoint into a dependable service. It includes the model block, attention and feed-forward kernels, model sharding, KV-cache allocation, request scheduling, batching, streaming, admission control, observability, and recovery.
lesson-production-transformer-architectu.example: In plain language: the checkpoint defines the math, while the production architecture decides where that math runs, which requests may run together, what state stays in memory, and what happens when demand or hardware breaks the plan.
lesson-production-transformer-architectu.takeaway: The core invariant is admitted work must fit the declared memory, latency, correctness, and availability envelope. High accelerator utilization is useful only while that contract remains true.

lesson-fine-tuning-practices.title: Fine-Tuning Best Practices
lesson-fine-tuning-practices.summary: Fine-tuning updates some or all parameters of a pretrained model so it performs a defined task more consistently. In supervised fine-tuning (SFT), each training record demonstrates the input the application will send and the output the model should produce.
lesson-fine-tuning-practices.example: In plain language: prompting tells a model what to do in one request; retrieval gives it current evidence; fine-tuning lets it practice a stable behavior across many examples. Those mechanisms solve different problems and can be combined.
lesson-fine-tuning-practices.takeaway: The production invariant is: a fine-tuned artifact ships only with a versioned task contract, representative held-out evidence, exact model-format lineage, and a tested rollback target.

models.title: Choose the smallest intervention that closes the measured gap

lesson-lora-fine-tuning.title: LoRA & Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
lesson-lora-fine-tuning.summary: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is a parameter-efficient way to specialize a pretrained model. The base model stays frozen. Training learns two much smaller matrices inside selected linear layers, and their product becomes a task-specific weight update.
lesson-lora-fine-tuning.example: In plain language: a team keeps one large foundation model and trains compact adapters for stable behaviors such as a response format, classification policy, or domain style. This reduces the parameters that need gradients, optimizer state, and separate checkpoint storage.
lesson-lora-fine-tuning.takeaway: The core invariant is: an adapter is a versioned delta against one exact base-model and input-format contract, not a portable model by itself.

models.title: Expose the real adapter and memory budget
Treat the adapter and runtime as one release contract

lesson-raft-fine-tuning.title: RAFT: Retrieval-Augmented Fine-Tuning
lesson-raft-fine-tuning.summary: Retrieval-Augmented Fine-Tuning (RAFT) is a supervised fine-tuning recipe for a language model that will answer questions with documents retrieved from a known domain. Each training record pairs a question with answer-bearing oracle documents, irrelevant or misleading distractor documents, and a target answer grounded in the oracle.
lesson-raft-fine-tuning.example: In plain language: ordinary RAG gives a model an open book at inference time. RAFT also lets the model practice using that kind of open book before deployment. It does not replace retrieval or guarantee correctness.
lesson-raft-fine-tuning.takeaway: The core invariant is: train and evaluate on the retrieval conditions the deployed generator must actually handle.

lesson-clip-architecture.title: CLIP Architecture & Applications
lesson-clip-architecture.summary: CLIP (Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training) is a dual-encoder model that learns which images and text descriptions belong together. One encoder turns an image into a vector, another turns text into a vector, and learned projections place both vectors in the same coordinate system.
lesson-clip-architecture.example: That shared space matters because a text query can be compared directly with millions of precomputed image vectors. The same model can support image retrieval and zero-shot classification without training a new classifier head for every label set.
lesson-clip-architecture.takeaway: A matching image and text should point in similar directions after projection and normalization; mismatched pairs should point in different directions. CLIP estimates compatibility in its training distribution. It does not prove that a statement is true, generate a caption, or understand every object relationship in a scene.

lesson-text-to-image.title: Text-to-Image Generation
lesson-text-to-image.summary: Text-to-image generation turns a written description into a newly synthesized image. A production pipeline encodes the prompt, starts from a noisy image representation, repeatedly predicts how to remove noise while consulting the prompt, and decodes the final representation into pixels.
lesson-text-to-image.example: In plain language: the model is not searching for a matching picture or drawing one object at a time. It is refining a field of noise into a candidate that should satisfy the requested subjects, attributes, relationships, and style.
lesson-text-to-image.takeaway: Core invariant: the prompt is a conditioning signal, not a pixel-level specification. Every candidate still needs evaluation against the intended composition, visual quality, safety policy, and release context.

Balance text intent with spatial control

lesson-diffusion-models-production.title: Diffusion Models for Production
lesson-diffusion-models-production.summary: A diffusion model is a generative model that learns to reverse a gradual noising process. At inference time, it starts with random noise and repeatedly predicts how to move that sample toward data that resembles its training distribution. Text-to-image systems add text conditioning so those updates also follow a prompt.
lesson-diffusion-models-production.example: In plain language: the service turns noise into an image through a sequence of model-guided corrections. Each correction consumes accelerator time, so production quality depends on both the learned model and the system that budgets, queues, checks, stores, and delivers those corrections.
lesson-diffusion-models-production.takeaway: The core invariant is bounded, attributable generation: every accepted job has a fixed model and sampling contract, a deadline and compute budget, an externally enforced publication policy, and enough versioned metadata to explain or replay the result.

models.title: Fit the denoising path inside one request envelope
Keep queue pressure and failure blast radius bounded

lesson-text-to-image-system-design.title: Text-to-Image System Design
lesson-text-to-image-system-design.summary: A text-to-image system turns a written intent into an image through a bounded generation job. The job combines text conditioning, a generative model, decoding, policy checks, storage, and delivery. Diffusion is a common generation method, but it is not the entire product.
lesson-text-to-image-system-design.example: The difficult system-design question is not simply "Which model makes the best image?" It is how to deliver useful images while GPU capacity, latency, safety, quality, provenance, and failure recovery remain measurable.
lesson-text-to-image-system-design.takeaway: Core invariant: a generation is complete only after the system records the job state, policy decision, model configuration, output identity, and durable delivery result. A decoded image without those facts is an ungoverned artifact, not a production result.

models.title: Fit image quality to a bounded GPU queue
Trace a candidate through the release gates

lesson-video-generation.title: Video Generation
lesson-video-generation.summary: Video generation is the use of a learned generative model to synthesize a sequence of related frames from text, images, video, motion controls, or a combination of those signals. The result is not just a stack of good images. It is a timeline in which subjects, scene state, motion, lighting, and camera behavior should evolve coherently.
lesson-video-generation.example: In plain language: an image model must make one moment believable. A video model must make every moment believable and make the changes between moments make sense.
lesson-video-generation.takeaway: The core invariant is controlled continuity. A subject should change when the brief calls for action, occlusion, or a shot cut, but it should not change accidentally because the model lost track of identity or scene state.

lesson-image-captioning.title: Image Captioning
lesson-image-captioning.summary: Image captioning turns visual evidence into a natural-language description. A captioning system first represents image regions or patches, then a language decoder generates words that describe objects, attributes, actions, text, and relationships.
lesson-image-captioning.example: In plain language: the system looks at an image and proposes what should be said about it. The proposal may support a screen reader, image search, catalog metadata, moderation review, or an editing workflow.
lesson-image-captioning.takeaway: The central invariant is stricter than "write a fluent sentence": every factual claim in a released caption must be supported by permitted image or context evidence. If the system cannot support a useful claim, omission, review, or no caption is safer than a confident invention.

lesson-multimodal-ai.title: Multi-Modal AI APIs & Applications
lesson-multimodal-ai.summary: Multimodal AI is a system that can interpret or generate more than one form of information, such as text, images, audio, and video. A useful system does more than attach several files to one prompt: it preserves what each source observed, aligns related evidence, and makes missing or contradictory evidence visible before an output is trusted.
lesson-multimodal-ai.example: This matters because many real tasks cross media boundaries. An invoice has printed layout and structured business records. A meeting has speech, speakers, slides, and an agenda. A safety review has spatial detail and events that unfold over time.
lesson-multimodal-ai.takeaway: Invariant: every consequential claim must remain traceable to the source evidence and transformation that produced it. If a modality is absent, sampled away, or in conflict, the output must not imply that the missing evidence was verified.

lesson-advanced-image-captioning.title: Advanced Image Captioning Systems
lesson-advanced-image-captioning.summary: Advanced image captioning is the controlled generation of useful language from visual evidence. A vision encoder represents the image, a language decoder proposes a sequence of words, and an evidence-and-policy layer decides which claims may be released.
lesson-advanced-image-captioning.example: In plain language, the system must do more than produce a fluent sentence. It must notice the right objects and relationships, choose details that fit the product's purpose, avoid turning model confidence into visual fact, and stop or ask for review when the evidence is weak.
lesson-advanced-image-captioning.takeaway: The core invariant is every released claim must be supported by permitted evidence and useful for the declared captioning task. A likely token, a wide beam, an attention map, or a strong reference-overlap score cannot establish that an object is present.

lesson-blip3-xgen-mm.title: BLIP-3 (xGen-MM) Architecture
lesson-blip3-xgen-mm.summary: BLIP-3, also called xGen-MM, is Salesforce AI Research's open framework and model family for building large multimodal models that read images and text in one sequence. It combines a vision encoder, a vision token sampler, and a pretrained language model. The 2024 paper reports 4B and 14B model variants, base and instruction-tuned checkpoints, training recipes, and released datasets.
lesson-blip3-xgen-mm.example: The important idea is not simply "attach a camera to a language model." An image can produce far more features than a language model can afford to read. BLIP-3 preserves useful visual detail with image patches, compresses every patch into a bounded set of visual tokens, and places those tokens beside text in their natural interleaved order.
lesson-blip3-xgen-mm.takeaway: Visual evidence must remain identifiable after compression and sequence assembly. If the sampler discards a small label, or image order is lost, the language model cannot recover that evidence by reasoning harder.

lesson-internvl3-architecture.title: InternVL3: Next-Gen Vision-Language Models
lesson-internvl3-architecture.summary: InternVL3 is a family of vision-language models: it turns images or video frames into visual tokens, places those tokens beside text, and lets a language model reason over the combined sequence. The published InternVL3 project describes dynamic image tiling and Variable Visual Position Encoding (V2PE) for handling flexible visual inputs.
lesson-internvl3-architecture.example: This matters because images are expensive context. A document page, a multi-image comparison, and a video clip can all ask the model to preserve more detail than the language model can afford to read at once. The engineering task is to decide which visual evidence earns tokens without exhausting latency, memory, or the context window.
lesson-internvl3-architecture.takeaway: Invariant: every visual token must retain enough source identity and spatial order for the downstream model to relate it to the right image, tile, or frame, while the complete multimodal prompt stays inside an explicit serving budget.

lesson-multimodal-moe-systems.title: Multimodal MoE Systems
lesson-multimodal-moe-systems.concept: What is a multimodal mixture-of-experts system?
lesson-multimodal-moe-systems.summary: A multimodal mixture-of-experts (MoE) system processes more than one input type, such as text and images, while activating only a small part of a much larger model for each token. A learned router scores a pool of expert networks and sends each token to one or a few experts.
lesson-multimodal-moe-systems.example: In plain language: text and visual tokens can share one model, but they do not all take the same compute path.
lesson-multimodal-moe-systems.takeaway: The core invariant is every admitted token must have a bounded, observable path through the sparse layer. Sparse activation saves compute only when routing, capacity, communication, and overflow behavior remain controlled. It does not mean the inactive expert weights disappear from memory.

lesson-document-parsing-systems.title: Document Parsing: DeDOC & Layout-Parser
lesson-document-parsing-systems.summary: Document parsing turns a PDF, image, form, or office file into structured records that software can search, validate, and act on. It may extract text, but it must also recover where each item appeared, how items relate, and which source region supports every result.
lesson-document-parsing-systems.example: This matters because a plain text dump destroys evidence. A total can become detached from its currency, a table cell can move under the wrong header, and a footer can be mistaken for body text. The core invariant is therefore: every extracted claim remains traceable to its page, region, parser version, and validation result.

lesson-production-document-extraction.title: Production Document Extraction Systems
lesson-production-document-extraction.summary: Production document extraction turns PDFs, images, and document bundles into structured records that downstream software can safely use. OCR may recover characters, but a production system must also decide which parser to run, whether every required page and field is present, where each value came from, and what to do when evidence is weak or contradictory.
lesson-production-document-extraction.example: The core invariant is: an extracted value is a candidate until a versioned policy accepts its source evidence, schema, and validation results. Accepted output should remain immutable; retries and model upgrades create new candidates that can be compared, reviewed, promoted, or rejected.
lesson-production-document-extraction.takeaway: This lesson builds on Document Parsing Systems, which introduces text, layout, tables, and field evidence. Here, the focus shifts to production routing, quality gates, provenance, recovery, and operations.

lesson-laion-aesthetics.title: LAION Aesthetics & Quality Scoring
lesson-laion-aesthetics.summary: LAION Aesthetics is a family of LAION-5B subsets selected with learned aesthetic predictors built on image embeddings. The predictor estimates preferences represented in its rating data; it does not measure universal beauty, caption truth, safety, consent, provenance, or permission to train.
lesson-laion-aesthetics.example: The broader engineering subject is multimodal dataset curation: turning a large, noisy candidate index into a versioned release manifest whose inclusion decisions can be reproduced, evaluated by slice, audited, and revised.
lesson-laion-aesthetics.takeaway: Never collapse independent quality, safety, provenance, and representation decisions into one score. Bind every signal and decision to exact content identity and a versioned release manifest.

lesson-evaluation-benchmarks-comprehensi.title: Comprehensive Evaluation Benchmarks
lesson-evaluation-benchmarks-comprehensi.concept: What is a comprehensive evaluation benchmark portfolio?
lesson-evaluation-benchmarks-comprehensi.summary: A comprehensive evaluation benchmark portfolio is a versioned set of tests and review methods used to decide whether a model is fit for one product release. It combines public benchmarks, product-shaped tasks, safety and reliability checks, and human review where judgment is necessary.
lesson-evaluation-benchmarks-comprehensi.example: It matters because a leaderboard score answers a narrow question under one protocol. A user-facing system must also work for its highest-value tasks, its critical user slices, and its failure boundaries. Invariant: a release claim is only as strong as the independent evidence for every behavior it promises; a high average cannot cancel a failed critical slice or contaminated holdout.
lesson-evaluation-benchmarks-comprehensi.takeaway: Use the full lesson’s worked examples and interactive labs to explore the trade-offs behind these questions.

lesson-llm-as-judge-evaluation.title: LLM-as-Judge Evaluation
lesson-llm-as-judge-evaluation.summary: LLM-as-judge evaluation uses a language model to apply a written rubric to another system's output. The judge might assign a score, compare two responses, explain a defect, or abstain when the evidence is insufficient.
lesson-llm-as-judge-evaluation.example: In plain language, it is an automated reviewer. It matters because product teams often need to inspect thousands of open-ended answers that do not have one exact reference string. A judge can make that review faster and more repeatable, but it cannot turn a subjective decision into objective truth.
lesson-llm-as-judge-evaluation.takeaway: The core invariant is a judge result is evidence about a declared rubric, not ground truth. Every reported score must remain traceable to the judge version, prompt, rubric, input order, output pair, calibration set, human reference process, and release policy that produced it.

lesson-long-context-evaluation.title: Long-Context Evaluation
lesson-long-context-evaluation.summary: Long-context evaluation measures whether a model can use the right evidence when an input contains many tokens. It varies input length, evidence position, task structure, distractors, and output requirements, then measures both answer quality and whether the answer is supported by the supplied context.
lesson-long-context-evaluation.example: It matters because an API limit answers only, "Will this request fit?" A product needs to know, "At what lengths and positions does this exact model, prompt, and serving path still retrieve, combine, cite, and act on evidence reliably?"
lesson-long-context-evaluation.takeaway: The core invariant is simple: the usable context window is the largest tested region in which every release-critical task and slice passes its predeclared quality, evidence-use, latency, and cost gates. It is measured, not inferred from the advertised maximum.

lesson-agentic-ai-evaluation.title: Agentic AI Evaluation
lesson-agentic-ai-evaluation.summary: Agentic AI evaluation is the practice of testing an AI system that observes, plans, calls tools, changes external state, and adapts over multiple steps. A normal model evaluation can score one answer. An agent evaluation must score the full trajectory and verify what actually happened outside the model.
lesson-agentic-ai-evaluation.example: It matters because an agent can write a convincing completion message after a tool failed, repeat a payment after an ambiguous timeout, or finish the task by crossing a permission boundary. Core invariant: never accept an agent's success claim without joining it to the task contract, complete action trace, policy decisions, and authoritative external state.
lesson-agentic-ai-evaluation.takeaway: Review AI agents for planning and tool-use foundations, and LLM-as-judge evaluation before delegating rubric decisions to another model.

lesson-production-evaluation-pipelines.title: Production Evaluation Pipelines
lesson-production-evaluation-pipelines.concept: What is a production evaluation pipeline?
lesson-production-evaluation-pipelines.summary: A production evaluation pipeline is a versioned decision system that tests an AI change before release and keeps measuring it after launch. It connects prompts, models, retrieval data, tools, scoring rules, human review, deployment controls, and production outcomes into one traceable evidence path.
lesson-production-evaluation-pipelines.example: It matters because a model can improve on an average offline score while becoming worse for one user group, slower under real traffic, unsafe on a critical case, or expensive enough to break the product. Core invariant: every promotion or rollback decision must be reproducible from the exact candidate, baseline, test evidence, scoring protocol, thresholds, and exposure state used at that moment.
lesson-production-evaluation-pipelines.takeaway: If benchmarks and scoring are new, review comprehensive evaluation benchmarks before designing the automation around them.

lesson-evaluation-platforms.title: LLM Evaluation Platforms & Tools
lesson-evaluation-platforms.summary: An evaluation platform is the system of record and execution layer for measuring an AI application's behavior. It stores versioned test cases, runs a specific application configuration, captures outputs and traces, applies automated and human judgments, and turns the resulting evidence into an engineering decision.
lesson-evaluation-platforms.example: It matters because a score without its dataset, prompt, model, tools, evaluator, and review policy cannot explain a regression or support a release. Invariant: every result must remain traceable to the exact evidence and configuration that produced it.
lesson-evaluation-platforms.takeaway: If benchmark and scoring concepts are new, begin with comprehensive evaluation benchmarks before selecting platform infrastructure.

Make evidence lineage part of the release gate

lesson-ai-evaluation-drift.title: AI Evaluation Drift
lesson-ai-evaluation-drift.summary: AI evaluation drift is the gap that opens when an evaluation suite no longer measures the behavior users experience in production. The application can change, production traffic can change, or the evaluator itself can change.
lesson-ai-evaluation-drift.example: In plain language: a familiar score can stop meaning the same thing. A safe evaluation system therefore versions the product, the evidence, and the judge, then compares important traffic slices before it makes a release decision.
lesson-ai-evaluation-drift.takeaway: Never interpret a score change until you can identify what was tested, which system produced the outputs, which population supplied the cases, and which evaluator produced the judgment.

lesson-common-sense-reasoning-benchmarks.title: Common Sense Reasoning: PIQA, HellaSwag & More
lesson-common-sense-reasoning-benchmarks.summary: Common-sense reasoning benchmarks are controlled question sets that probe whether a model can choose a plausible conclusion using everyday physical, social, causal, temporal, or relational knowledge. They usually present a short context and a small set of answer choices, which makes scoring repeatable but narrows what the result can prove.
lesson-common-sense-reasoning-benchmarks.example: They matter because fluent text can still violate basic expectations: a tool may not fit the task, an event continuation may be impossible, or a pronoun may resolve to the wrong person. Invariant: a benchmark score supports only the capability, item distribution, answer format, and evaluation protocol that produced it. It does not establish general common sense or product readiness by itself.
lesson-common-sense-reasoning-benchmarks.takeaway: Use the full lesson’s worked examples and interactive labs to explore the trade-offs behind these questions.

lesson-world-knowledge-benchmarks.title: World Knowledge: TriviaQA, NQ & SQuAD
lesson-world-knowledge-benchmarks.concept: What is a world knowledge benchmark?
lesson-world-knowledge-benchmarks.summary: A world knowledge benchmark is a versioned question set, evidence contract, answer format, and scoring rule used to measure whether a system can find and return factual information. Some tests ask a model to recall a fact, some provide or retrieve documents, and some require the system to abstain when the evidence does not contain an answer.
lesson-world-knowledge-benchmarks.example: In plain language, these benchmarks are different kinds of open-book and closed-book exams. They matter because a correct-looking answer can come from memorization, successful retrieval, careful reading, or luck. Those paths fail for different reasons.
lesson-world-knowledge-benchmarks.takeaway: The core invariant is match the benchmark's evidence contract to the product claim. A passage-reading score does not prove broad factual recall, and an end-to-end retrieval score does not isolate reader quality.

Diagnose the stage that loses the answer

lesson-mathematical-reasoning-benchmarks.title: Mathematical Reasoning: MATH & GSM8K
lesson-mathematical-reasoning-benchmarks.concept: What is a mathematical reasoning benchmark?
lesson-mathematical-reasoning-benchmarks.summary: A mathematical reasoning benchmark is a versioned set of problems, prompts, answer rules, and scoring procedures used to measure how reliably a model solves mathematical tasks. MATH focuses on competition-style problems across several subjects and difficulty levels. GSM8K focuses on linguistically varied, multi-step grade-school word problems.
lesson-mathematical-reasoning-benchmarks.example: In plain language, these benchmarks are controlled exams. They matter because a model can sound mathematically fluent while choosing the wrong operation, losing a constraint, making an arithmetic error, or formatting an equivalent answer in a way that a brittle grader rejects.
lesson-mathematical-reasoning-benchmarks.takeaway: The core invariant is same task set, same prompt contract, same decoding budget, and same verifier. A score is evidence about that frozen experiment, not proof that the model understands mathematics generally or that a generated explanation faithfully exposes its internal reasoning.

models.title: Separate answer correctness from trace diagnosis
Design the benchmark portfolio around the claim

lesson-code-generation-benchmarks.title: Code Generation: HumanEval & MBPP
lesson-code-generation-benchmarks.concept: What is a code generation benchmark?
lesson-code-generation-benchmarks.summary: A code generation benchmark is a repeatable experiment that asks a model to produce programs, runs those programs against a fixed test contract, and reports how often at least one sampled program succeeds. HumanEval and MBPP are two Python-oriented benchmark collections that make this experiment convenient.
lesson-code-generation-benchmarks.example: In plain language, the benchmark is an executable exam, not a syntax check. It matters because fluent-looking code can be wrong, slow, unsafe, or only tailored to the examples it saw. A result helps compare candidates only when every candidate receives the same tasks, runtime, sampling budget, tests, and scoring rule.
lesson-code-generation-benchmarks.takeaway: The core invariant is same untrusted workload, same versioned test contract: the score must be reproducible from the frozen task revision, generation settings, sandbox policy, and per-candidate test outcomes. A high pass@k is not evidence that generated code is safe to run outside that boundary.

models.title: Design the pass@k claim before sampling
Gate execution, security, and evidence separately

lesson-composite-benchmarks-mmlu.title: Composite Benchmarks: MMLU, MMMU & AGIEval
lesson-composite-benchmarks-mmlu.summary: MMLU, or Massive Multitask Language Understanding, is a text-only benchmark that asks four-option multiple-choice questions across 57 academic and professional subjects. It gives every response an unambiguous correctness label, then summarizes how often a model selected the reference answer.
lesson-composite-benchmarks-mmlu.example: In plain language, MMLU is a broad, standardized exam for a language model. It matters because one frozen test can expose uneven knowledge across mathematics, history, law, medicine, computer science, and many other subjects. It is useful for comparing model versions under the same protocol.
lesson-composite-benchmarks-mmlu.takeaway: The core invariant is same evidence, same procedure: a score is comparable only when the dataset version, prompt, demonstrations, answer ordering, decoding settings, and answer extractor are held constant. The overall percentage must remain traceable to per-subject counts and uncertainty.

models.title: See how an overall score can hide a domain failure
